# Signing the panel references

Fourteen panels, each with a light and a dark rendering, and **a machine drew
every one of them.** `panels/README.md` says why that matters: the check cannot
tell a reference somebody studied from one a machine drew unattended, which is
the whole reason the name is written by hand.

**Ticking a box in this file signs nothing.** The attestation is the
`confirmed_by` line in `panels/<id>.toml` and nowhere else. This page is a
reading aid; the boxes are for keeping your place.

## What a machine has already established

- All fourteen pass `tools/panel_check.py`: they render, they move, they read
  the rows they declare, and each matches its own stored reference.
- Every number printed inside a figure is computed from the arrays that figure
  is drawn from. None is typed. That makes them self-consistent; it does not
  make them right, which is what a reader is for.

## What only a person can do

Open both pictures and read the claim below them. Two things to look for in a
dark rendering that the light one will never show: a block of light where a
fill should have gone dark, and a line you have to hunt for. Both are one
defect — a value chosen against the wrong surface — and both pass every
mechanical check in this repository.

## To sign one

In `panels/<id>.toml`, replace the `confirmed_by` line with your name, the
date, and which renderings you looked at:

```toml
confirmed_by = "A. Rai / 2026-09-20 (light and dark both looked at)"
```

Then `tools/panel_review.py` to refresh this file, and commit both. Signing a
panel you have not opened is worse than leaving it UNCONFIRMED: the field
exists so a later reader knows which references were studied.

To look at them all at once:

```
tools/panel_review.py --sheets /tmp/sheets
```

---

**11 of 14 panels are UNCONFIRMED.** `matrix`, `paths`, `tree` carry no `confirmed_by` field at all —
those three predate the field and it was deliberately never backfilled, because
nobody now remembers who looked and a guessed attestation is worse than none.

## `closure` — Closure — each requirement against what the record gives it

- [ ] light — `panels/reference/closure.png`
- [ ] dark — `panels/reference/closure.dark.png`

<details><summary>what it must show (<code>correct</code>)</summary>

```
A DARK RENDERING IS RECORDED BESIDE THE LIGHT ONE and both have to be looked at.
The canvas gets none of CSS's help: its palette is a second table in
web/js/chart.js, chosen and validated against the dark surface separately, so
it can be wrong in ways the light one is not. What to check is the same in both
— every claim above — plus one thing only the dark picture can show: nothing in
the frame should be a light block. A literal light fill that never followed the
scheme reads as a hole burned in the page.

THE FINDING LINE IS THE CHECK ABOVE, MADE BY THE PANEL. The crossing in the top
frame is computed from the achieved curve and the requirement line; the crossing
in the bottom one from the margin. They come from different arrays, and the
finding states that they agree — or, in capitals, that they do NOT, which is the
defect this block describes and nothing else could catch.

TWO FRAMES on one shared x axis, its ticks and title drawn once at the bottom.
The top frame carries two lines in the same unit: a swept curve and a flat
dashed one. THE REQUIREMENT LINE MUST BE FLAT — it is a declared number a
person chose, and a requirement that slopes means the panel is sweeping the
bound instead of the environment. The bottom frame carries one line with a red
zero rule on it.

The two frames must agree: wherever the swept curve crosses the requirement in
the top frame, the margin crosses zero in the bottom one, at the same x. They
are the same fact twice and a picture where the crossings are at different
places has computed the margin from something other than the two lines above
it.

THE AREA BETWEEN THE TWO LINES IS FILLED AND IT CHANGES COLOUR AT THE CROSSING.
Left of the crossing the fill is the achieved curve's own hue and it is margin
left; right of it the fill is the pink every bound in this face is drawn in and
it is requirement exceeded. The two meet exactly at the crossing and nowhere
else — one fill in one colour across the whole span is the defect, because it
draws "this much is unspent" and "this much is overspent" as the same wedge.
The bottom frame washes everything below zero in the same pink, and the wash
must start at the same x the top frame's pink fill does.

The margin is POSITIVE where the achieved curve is BELOW the requirement,
because every one of these five declares sense "<=" — the requirement is a
ceiling and room is what is left under it. A margin that rises as the achieved
curve rises has the sense backwards.

The horizontal axis must NOT be the pair's own requirement. A margin is a
fraction of its bound, so sweeping the bound moves the margin by construction
and says nothing about the sky; /v1/levers reports the requirement at or near
the top of every one of these five, and the panel is required to skip it. An
axis labelled "Required — ..." is that defect.

Switching the closure control must change the axis as well as the curves: the
two F10.7 pairs are spent fastest by the mean band spread, the survival pair by
mission duration, and the two sustained/daily Ap pairs by the expected Ap over
the window. An axis that stays the same across all five means the lever
question is not being asked.
```

</details>

## `design` — Design — the window against what the vehicle is built for

- [ ] light — `panels/reference/design.png`
- [ ] dark — `panels/reference/design.dark.png`

<details><summary>what it must show (<code>correct</code>)</summary>

```
A DARK RENDERING IS RECORDED BESIDE THE LIGHT ONE and both have to be looked at.
The canvas gets none of CSS's help: its palette is a second table in
web/js/chart.js, chosen and validated against the dark surface separately, so
it can be wrong in ways the light one is not. What to check is the same in both
— every claim above — plus one thing only the dark picture can show: nothing in
the frame should be a light block. A literal light fill that never followed the
scheme reads as a hole burned in the page.

the finding line says where the curve enters the shaded region and where it
reaches the requirement, both read off the drawn curve by interpolation.

The record's expectation as a curve, with the selected capability and the
selected requirement drawn as marks that sit at their stated values on the same
axis — at G3 the capability is Ap 132, and the requirement mark moves when the
requirement control does. Where the expectation crosses the capability is the
number sw_design_safe_duration publishes, and it is labelled AT THE CROSSING —
a dot on the curve with a short leader to "exceeded here", carrying the year.
It used to be a dashed rule the full height of the frame with its label at the
ceiling, which is a fact about a point told somewhere else. A vertical rule
here is the defect now. Both marks carry labels naming what
they are; two unlabelled horizontal lines are the defect this catches.

EVERYTHING ABOVE THE CAPABILITY IS WASHED, in the capability mark's own colour
and not the requirement's. The wash opens at the capability line and runs to
the top of the frame, so which side of the line is the bad side is something a
reader sees rather than works out. A wash drawn in the requirement's pink while
opening at the capability is the defect to look for: a region belongs to the
edge it opens at.

ON THE F10.7 BRANCH, which the reference image does not cover because it is
shot at the state the panel opens in: FIVE curves against mission length. Four
solid ones are the design rows — hot and cold, sustained and single day — and
they are nested in that order and never cross, because each cold value is below
its hot counterpart by construction. All four WANDER up and down with mission
length; a monotone set here means they are being read off something other than
the window mean.

The fifth is DASHED AND DRAWN AT HALF CONTRAST, and is not a design value: sw_window_peak_level is the
maximum of the same cycle analogue the other four are built on a mean of. It
must rise MONOTONICALLY and in steps — a longer window can only contain more of
the cycle, and the peak jumps when the window swallows another cycle maximum, so
a smooth or falling dashed line is the defect. It crosses ABOVE the hot
single-day curve at about 5.9 years, and that crossing is the point of drawing
it: past there the design is sized on a mean that sits under the thing it
averages.

The area between the hot single-day curve and the cold single-day curve is
FILLED: that area is the design window, which the note has always called it and
the picture used to leave as two edges a reader subtracted. The fill is bounded
by the outer two curves and by nothing else — a fill reaching the sustained
curves instead would be drawing the wrong window. The band above the
requirement is washed in the same pink the requirement line is drawn in.
```

</details>

## `drivers` — Drivers — the five scenarios, against the legacy run

- [ ] light — `panels/reference/drivers.png`
- [ ] dark — `panels/reference/drivers.dark.png`

<details><summary>what it must show (<code>correct</code>)</summary>

```
A DARK RENDERING IS RECORDED BESIDE THE LIGHT ONE and both have to be looked at.
The canvas gets none of CSS's help: its palette is a second table in
web/js/chart.js, chosen and validated against the dark surface separately, so
it can be wrong in ways the light one is not. What to check is the same in both
— every claim above — plus one thing only the dark picture can show: nothing in
the frame should be a light block. A literal light fill that never followed the
scheme reads as a hole burned in the page.

the finding line says at how many scenarios this tree sits below the legacy run,
and whether its own line rises across all five. Both are counted, so a ladder
that stopped being monotone would say so rather than being described as rising.

THE FRAME IS NARROWER THAN THE OTHERS AND THAT IS DELIBERATE. Five categories
cannot use 1180 pixels of width: stretched across a full frame the scenario
ladder becomes a shallow diagonal, which is the banking argument fitCanvas was
written for, running the other way. The spec asks for width ÷ height = 1.5, so
the picture is about 806 wide. A full-width drivers frame is the previous form.

THE WIDEST GAP CARRIES A NOTE at the legacy dot it happens on, saying WHY the
two methods part there — one percentile applied at every level on the
single-day scenarios, a differently centred window on the sustained ones. Which
scenario that is comes from the data, not from a list here.

NO VERTICAL GRIDLINES. This axis is five named scenarios, and a gridline is an
invitation to read a value off the axis where it falls — between "cold
sustained" and "nominal" there is nothing to read. The horizontal grid stays,
because the y axis IS a scale. A vertical rule at the first scenario is the
specific defect to look for: the axis runs -0.3 to 4.3, so a zero rule kept
"because zero matters" lands on a category and is drawn darker than a gridline.

In the by-quantity view: a rising line of five points, because the scenarios are
ordered cold to hot and every quantity here is monotone in that order. A line
that zigzags means the scenarios have been drawn in the order the CSV lists them
rather than in the order a design reads them. Five DOTS from the legacy run sit
on the same five x positions; where the two agree the dot sits on the line.

On Ap and on both Kp quantities the dot sits ON the line at the three SUSTAINED
scenarios — nominal, cold sustained, hot sustained — and well off it at the two
single-day scenarios, high at the worst day and low at the quietest. That
asymmetry is the finding, not a defect: the study applies one within-rotation
percentile everywhere and this port conditions it on the level it applies at, so
the two diverge in opposite directions at the two ends. A picture where the
single-day dots also sit on the line means the level-conditioned table is not
being read.

On F10.7 and on the 81-day mean the legacy dots sit ABOVE the line at every
scenario, by roughly a factor of two. The two tools centre the window
differently — the study holds its last rotation forecast flat at 158.33 sfu and
this port reads the cycle analogue at the declared epoch and gets 86.85 — and
that is a decision §20 took, not an error to reconcile.

In the parity view: five lines on a LOGARITHMIC axis with a red line at one.
NINE of the twenty-five points must sit on that line to within a tenth of a per
cent, and they are a block rather than a scatter: daily Ap, Kp mean and Kp peak
at each of the three SUSTAINED scenarios. The worst departure is daily Ap at the
worst day, a factor of 2.18. If all twenty-five sit on the line the panel is
dividing a number by itself and not reading the legacy file at all; if none do,
it is not reading the engine. The axis must be logarithmic — on a linear one a
ratio of 2 and a ratio of 0.5 are different distances from agreement, which is
the wrong claim about two errors of the same size.
```

</details>

## `forecast` — Forecast — the issued outlook, scored

- [ ] light — `panels/reference/forecast.png`
- [ ] dark — `panels/reference/forecast.dark.png`

<details><summary>what it must show (<code>correct</code>)</summary>

```
A DARK RENDERING IS RECORDED BESIDE THE LIGHT ONE and both have to be looked at.
The canvas gets none of CSS's help: its palette is a second table in
web/js/chart.js, chosen and validated against the dark surface separately, so
it can be wrong in ways the light one is not. What to check is the same in both
— every claim above — plus one thing only the dark picture can show: nothing in
the frame should be a light block. A literal light fill that never followed the
scheme reads as a hole burned in the page.

the finding line counts the leads at which the strict skill line is above zero,
the leads at which the leaky one is, and the leads at which the bias frame is
below zero. Three counts, all made at draw time, and the gap between the first
two is the leak this panel exists to show.

THREE FRAMES IN A COLUMN on the by-lead and by-year views, sharing one
horizontal axis with its ticks and title drawn ONCE at the bottom. Each frame
carries its own y label and its own scale; a single y axis across all three, or
two scales in one frame, is the defect to look for. A vertical read down the
stack must land on the same lead in every frame — the frames are registered on
one x extent, so a crosshair crossing all three at different leads means they
have been scaled separately.

The zero line is drawn and labelled on BOTH difference metrics. Skill is
against a baseline and bias is a signed error, so neither can be read without
the value that means "no difference" on the picture; RMS error gets no line,
because it is a magnitude that cannot go negative and zero there is perfection
rather than a baseline. The bias frame is the one to check hardest: with the
line drawn, the by-lead series is visibly below it at EVERY lead, which is the
outlook under-predicting F10.7 throughout.

THE SKILL FRAME WASHES EVERYTHING BELOW ZERO AND THE BIAS FRAME DOES NOT, and
that asymmetry is deliberate. On the skill frame zero is a verdict — below it
the outlook is worse than not bothering — so the side is worth saying without
being read. On the bias frame zero is a direction rather than a verdict, and
the bias is negative at all 27 leads, so a wash there would cover the whole
frame: a frame that is entirely shaded has said nothing. A bias frame washed
below zero is the defect to look for.

THE SKILL FRAME CARRIES TWO LINES and the dashed one must sit BELOW the solid
one at short lead. Solid is the strict baseline — the last observation before
the issue date, what a forecaster actually had — and the outlook beats it from
lead 1, peaking near +0.44 around lead 9 and going negative only at leads 23 to
25. Dashed is the leaky baseline, which is handed the issue date itself; it
makes persistence look better, so skill against it collapses at short lead. Two
lines that agree everywhere means the leak is not being computed.

THE RMS FRAME STARTS AT ZERO AND ITS AREA IS FILLED. RMS error is a magnitude
measured from perfect rather than a score against a baseline, so zero is the
origin the quantity is a size from; an axis starting at 9 drew the VARIATION in
the error and labelled it the error. With zero on the frame the picture says the
error roughly triples over the first five leads and then flattens, which is the
claim. A fill under either of the other two frames is the defect — neither is a
size from zero.

THE LEAKY BASELINE IS DRAWN AT HALF CONTRAST. The strict baseline is the score
this panel publishes; the leaky one is there to show what the leak is worth, and
at equal weight it competed with the number. Two skill lines at one weight is the
state to look for.

Bias and RMS error have ONE line each and no baseline variant, because neither
uses a baseline. They are also computed over every pair with an observation
rather than over the pairs a baseline happened to reach, so their sample is
larger than the skill frame's — a panel where all three frames rest on the
identical count has tied a baseline-free metric to a baseline again.

ON THE BY-CALENDAR-YEAR VIEW the horizontal axis is the year of ISSUE and every
line BREAKS at every year dropped for thinness — 1997, 2000, 2009, 2010 and
2017. A continuous line across those is the defect to look for: it would draw
two years of evidence where the archive holds 25 pairs. The skill series dips
below the red line once, at 2008, and that is the record behaving rather than
the outlook failing — a flat minimum is the easy case for persistence, and the
RMS frame beneath it confirms it by showing that year as the smallest error in
the series. Every year is scored on leads 1 to 14 only, which is the band every
year populates; a version scoring all leads together would rank 2004 and 2007
highly for holding no long leads at all.

The lead axis runs 1 to 27, which is the outlook's nominal span and NOT the
same number as sw_outlook_lead's 26. The bundle carries leads from -26 to 392,
so drawing 1 to 27 is a deliberate restriction to the issued window; the row
publishes 26 because that is the longest lead most issues actually index. The
two disagree on purpose and a reviewer should not reconcile them by moving
either.
```

</details>

## `pattern` — Pattern — recurrence at the solar rotation

- [ ] light — `panels/reference/pattern.png`
- [ ] dark — `panels/reference/pattern.dark.png`

<details><summary>what it must show (<code>correct</code>)</summary>

```
A DARK RENDERING IS RECORDED BESIDE THE LIGHT ONE and both have to be looked at.
The canvas gets none of CSS's help: its palette is a second table in
web/js/chart.js, chosen and validated against the dark surface separately, so
it can be wrong in ways the light one is not. What to check is the same in both
— every claim above — plus one thing only the dark picture can show: nothing in
the frame should be a light block. A literal light fill that never followed the
scheme reads as a hole burned in the page.

the finding line reads "the 731-day curve sits above the 365-day one at 182 of the
200 lags, and the 365 curve is outside the band at N of them". Both counts are
made at draw time — 182 is not typed anywhere — and the first is this view's own
claim above, now countable rather than asserted.

THE 365-DAY CURVE IS THE ONLY ONE AT FULL CONTRAST. It is the window
sw_recurrence_lag and sw_recurrence_strength were measured under, and the one
the band and all three peak marks are computed on; 181 and 731 are drawn at
half contrast because their job is to show that the published number is a
CHOICE. All three stay readable — the 731-above-365 claim below is checked by
looking.

In the recurrence view: THREE curves, one per detrend window, all starting at
lag 1 and decaying, oscillating rather than falling smoothly, with weaker
repeats near the multiples. The 365-day curve is the heavy one and the 731-day
curve sits ABOVE it at 182 of the 200 lags — a longer detrend window calls less
of the record trend, so more low-frequency signal survives into the residual and
every correlation is higher. A picture where 731 sits below 365 through the
rotation band has the two windows crossed. Three NOTES, not three rules: the first local maximum and its second and third
harmonics, each a dot on the 365 curve with a leader to a label. The second and
third carry the period they IMPLY — the lag divided by 2 and by 3 — and both
must read about 27.0 days per cycle. That division is the argument of this
view, and it was a sentence underneath a frame where the three marks said only
where they were. Full-height dashed rules here are the previous form. The first reads 26
days, not 27: the nominal synodic rotation is 27 and the record's own
autocorrelation peaks at 26, which is what sw_recurrence_lag publishes and a
discrepancy a reviewer should weigh rather than round away. A panel that marked
27 here would be agreeing with the textbook instead of with the record. Every
curve stays within -1 and 1, because they are correlations. A dashed grey band
sits symmetrically about zero and WIDENS with lag; a band of constant width is
the naive white-noise interval and not what is claimed. That band is FILLED
between its two edges, not merely outlined, so "inside the band" is an area a
curve is visibly in or out of rather than a pair of dashed lines a reader holds
in mind; the edges stay, because an area with no boundary invites reading its
top as a maximum. The horizontal axis
ends at 200 and the curves reach it. In the spike view the picture is a scatter
rather than a curve, and no autocorrelation axis remains.
```

</details>

```
— every claim above — plus one thing only the dark picture can show: nothing in
the frame should be a light block. A literal light fill that never followed the
scheme reads as a hole burned in the page.

the finding line names the 95th’s hump, its dip and the rise after, with the
value and lead of each; where there is no hump — on Ap — it reports how far the
fan opens between the shortest lead and the longest instead.

FOUR curves of percentile change against lead, nested and never crossing: the
99th is the topmost everywhere and the 50th the lowest, because they are
quantiles of one sample and a crossing would mean they were read off different
ones. They are four steps of ONE hue, light for the 50th to dark for the 99th,
never four different colours — an ordered set drawn in categorical hues says
the four are unrelated. The 95th is the heavy line. The horizontal axis ends at
the last lead in the ladder and NOT at fifteen years: the ladder is geometric
and its last rung is 13.54 years, and an axis that stopped exactly on fifteen
would mean the ladder had been resampled to be tidy. The curves are measured,
not fitted: at short leads they wobble rather than rising smoothly, and the
95th stops being monotone altogether — it rises to 116 sfu at 4.08 years, falls
to 64 at 10.03, and rises again, which is the eleven-year cycle showing
through. The four never cross: they are quantiles of one sorted sample at each
lead, so a crossing is the sample having been rebuilt per percentile. A smooth monotone curve means something has
been fitted. Every line FADES toward the long leads, because the pair count
falls away and a line of constant weight would claim the far end is as well
known as the near one. THE FAN IS FILLED between the 50th and the 99th, in the published
percentile's own hue and under all four lines. That area is what choosing a
percentile costs, and it must OPEN with the lead: a fill of roughly constant
width means the percentiles are not spreading and something has been fitted.
The fill carries no legend entry — it is the spread of the family the four
lines are, not a fifth quantity.

TWO NOTES SIT ON THE 95TH, at its mid-lead hump and its late dip, naming them
as half a solar cycle and a full one. They are found by searching the curve
between 3 and 6 years and between 9 and 12 — never typed — so a label cannot
drift from the point under it, and they are drawn ONLY where the hump is
actually higher than the late maximum. On Ap, where it is not, there are no
notes and that is correct rather than missing.

Splitting by cycle replaces the four with one curve per
cycle, at the 95th.
```

```
what makes the mean legible AS a mean. Five curves at one weight is the state
§34 measured — no entry point, and the reader told in prose which line the
panel is about. They must still be readable enough to check the claim in the

escapes them is an averaging error. Cycle 25 may sit outside it, and does,
since it is excluded from the average. Cycle 25's line is dashed and ends before
phase 1 while the others do not. The vertical axis is labelled with the
selected variable and its unit, and changing the variable changes that label.
```

## `thermosphere` — Thermosphere — where the solar drivers become physics

- [ ] light — `panels/reference/thermosphere.png`
- [ ] dark — `panels/reference/thermosphere.dark.png`

<details><summary>what it must show (<code>correct</code>)</summary>

```
A DARK RENDERING IS RECORDED BESIDE THE LIGHT ONE and both have to be looked at.
The canvas gets none of CSS's help: its palette is a second table in
web/js/chart.js, chosen and validated against the dark surface separately, so
it can be wrong in ways the light one is not. What to check is the same in both
— every claim above — plus one thing only the dark picture can show: nothing in
the frame should be a light block. A literal light fill that never followed the
scheme reads as a hole burned in the page.

each view carries a finding line counting what it claims: where the three flux
relations meet and the two slopes, how far apart the two lightest Kp curves ever
get, whether the worst-slot line is above the mean-slot one at every scenario,
and where the measured geomagnetic curve separates from its own straight line.

EVERY NUMBER AND EVERY SLOPE COMES FROM THE ENGINE. No coefficient of the
relation appears in the panel's source, so the first thing to check is that the
measured slopes in the first view agree with the sheet: a SUSTAINED rise must
read 3.24 K per sfu, a single day departing from a fixed 81-day mean 1.30, and
the 81-day mean moving under a fixed day 1.94. Those are the sheet's own
coefficients recovered from three sweeps, and if the panel ever carried them as
literals this check would pass while meaning nothing.

IN THE FIRST VIEW the three lines must CROSS at a single point, and that point
is where env_f107 and env_f107a are both declared — 150. There is no departure
there, so all three relations agree, and three lines that cross at three
different places mean one of the sweeps is being taken somewhere else. Two
vertical marks: the declared 150, and what the solar subsystem computes for its
hot sustained scenario, which is lower. The distance between those two marks is
§28.2 and it is the reason this panel exists, and it is WASHED between them
rather than left as two ticks a reader subtracts. The wash has two measured
ends and both are named by the marks it runs between; an open-ended wash here
would be claiming a bound one of them does not have.

IN THE SECOND VIEW five curves, one per scenario, ordered cold to hot as five
steps of ONE hue — never five different colours, because the scenarios are a
ladder and a rainbow across them says they are unrelated things. All five bend
UPWARD with Kp; a straight set means the exponential is not being drawn. Two
dots sit on each curve, at that scenario's mean-slot and peak-slot Kp, and the
right-hand dot is always the higher. The two lightest curves nearly coincide and
that is the data: the quietest day rides on the cold sustained level and barely
departs from it.

IN THE FOURTH VIEW the axis starts at zero and the area under the measured curve
is FILLED, because the quantity is a temperature the geomagnetic term ADDS and
that area is the quantity. The straight reference line is drawn at half contrast:
it is what the curve is measured against, not a second measurement.

IN THE THIRD VIEW the frame is NARROWER than the others — five named scenarios
do not need 1180 pixels of width, and stretched across a full frame the gap
this view exists to show flattens. Two lines across the five scenarios, the worst-slot one above
the mean-slot one everywhere, with the gap WIDENING toward the hot end. A
constant gap would mean the exponential is missing. The worst-slot line must NOT
be drawn in #c2185b: that colour is what this face uses for a line a value is
measured against, and a data series wearing it reads as a threshold.

IN THE FOURTH VIEW two lines from the same sweep, coincident at the quiet end
and separating above about Kp 5, with the measured one ABOVE the straight one —
it is an exponential added to a linear term, so it can only depart upward. Both
must start at exactly zero at Kp 0, because the quantity drawn is the swept
answer minus its own value there.

ACROSS THE SECOND AND THIRD VIEWS the worst-day gap must be the SAME NUMBER in
both notes. They are two pictures of one fact, and they disagreed by half a
kelvin until the dots stopped being read off a 46-point sweep and became runs of
the engine at the exact Kp.
```

</details>
